question: to the Commission Lara Magoni (ECR) Subject:

Fraud associated with the cultural and creative content generated by artificial intelligence is a systemic challenge to the entire European creative sector, including music, the visual arts, graphic design, audiovisual works, digital publishing and podcasts. Bots, automated traffic and manipulative practices can be used to generate large-scale artificial listening, viewing and interaction, hence altering algorithms, rankings and remuneration systems. These practices deprive legitimate creators of revenue and visibility, diminish content pluralism and undermine consumer trust, leading to a distorted market. For example, in the music sector, around 10 % of the new tracks uploaded each day are generated by AI, of which 85 % are fraudulent, which goes to show the scale of the phenomenon. Such practices violate Article 50 of the AI Act, which states that AI-generated content must be clearly identifiable to ensure transparency, fairness and copyright protection. In the light of this damage to a key sector of Europe’s economy and identity, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
How will it ensure the transparent and uniform implementation of the obligations arising from the AI Act in the digital creative sector?
What measures is it considering to ensure economic protection, visibility and recognition for bona fide creators and to strengthen consumer trust in the EU digital market?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The AI Act1 includes transparency obligations to support distinguishing AI-generated content from human content. The AI Office facilitated the development of a Code of Practice2 as a voluntary tool to support compliance with those obligations; the final version of the Code was published on 10 June 2026. The AI Office will also issue guidelines on those obligations, which it intends to adopt by August 2026. Furthermore, providers placing General Purpose AI (GPAI) models on the EU market must put in place a policy to comply with EU copyright law and disclose detailed summaries of training data. To support the implementation of these provisions, a template for a public summary of training content has been developed3, together with a Code of Practice for GPAI models4, to assist providers in complying with those obligations, including identifying and respecting reservations of rights expressed by rightsholders in a machine-readable format and mitigating the risk of copyright-infringing outputs. The Commission is facilitating a process to identify technical solutions for machine readable rights reservation (beyond robot.txt). Under the Apply AI Strategy5, the commission will also launch a study on legal challenges and technological safeguards against copyright-infringing AI outputs. The Commission monitors market and technological developments affecting the cultural and creative sectors and will, if necessary, use its powers, including under EU competition law, to ensure a level playing field. Furthermore, the Commission recently published a study on the discoverability of diverse European content online6 and will present a dedicated AI strategy for the cultural and creative sectors.
